core.text: Concrete control: validate N3,N4,N5,N6,N7,N8 at ticks 0,1,2,3,4,5. Request individual N2,N3,N4,N5 at ticks 0,1,2,3; bulk at 5; individual N8 at 6. Predicted deliveries are N2,N3,N4,N5 at ticks 1,2,3,4, idle at 5, N6,N7,N8 at 6,7,8. Together with initial N1, this predicts eight recognitions and registrations.

Present harm regime: replace only the tick-0 individual request with bulk, increasing bulk interventions from one to two within the same six actions. Predicted tick-1 N1 duplicate delays N5 delivery to tick 5, when the unchanged bulk request captures still-pending N5. Its duplicate consumes tick 6; N6 and N7 deliver at 7 and 8, leaving N8 queued beyond the window. Predicted recognition count falls to seven.

Predeclared detector: at least two nonprogress server slots among ticks 1 through 8, counting duplicates, failures, or idle ticks. Eight slots must supply seven new distinct recognitions, so two nonprogress slots force failure. Control predicts one idle slot; increased bulk predicts two duplicates. This threshold is fixed before observing results.

Separating probe: replay the two stipulated schedules from identical starting states; change only the tick-0 request type. Compare registrations, pending identities, FIFO entries, first deliveries, and boundary-9 distinct recognitions. Defeat: increased bulk achieves eight recognitions or lacks the predicted duplicates under these fixed controls. Each arm uses six validation ticks and six dispatcher actions; ledger reads add no clerk labor.

residue.text: Registration independently enables requests; bulk increases queued receipts without increasing validation or server capacity. Both arms predict eight registrations, so recognition failure cannot be hidden by registration success. Extra capacity and repair are unavailable.

N8 availability remains inconvenient: delivery must occur at ticks 6 through 8. The proposed control predicts tick 8; the increased-bulk arm loses this slot. These are finite-model predictions, not observed executions or a globally optimal schedule proof.

The exceptional display-delay origin, empirical network distribution, and later sender adaptation remain unknown. No new demand occurs here; hypothetical later status traffic does not establish this present harm boundary.

tension.account_a: FIFO interference: increased bulk intervention turns delayed pending displays into duplicate service work, reducing present distinct recognition.
tension.account_b: Batching benefit: more bulk coverage improves acknowledgment efficiency; the stale display has no outcome cost within these controls.
tension.prediction_a: Identical registrations; increased bulk yields duplicates at ticks 1 and 6 and seven recognitions versus control eight.
tension.prediction_b: Increased bulk preserves eight recognitions by boundary 9 despite the stale display.
